clips.send: Greensboro sit-ins. 1 February 1960, Greensboro, North Carolina. Four Black college students sat at the “whites only” lunch counter at Woolworth’s and politely asked to be served. They were refused — and came back the next day with more students. Sit-ins (静坐) spread to dozens of cities within weeks. In April, students founded SNCC (the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee). In July 1960 the Greensboro Woolworth’s served Black customers at the counter. Part of that counter is now in the Smithsonian.

clips.send: Brown v. Board of Education. 17 May 1954, Topeka, Kansas. Linda Brown, a Black third-grader, had to travel far to a Black school although a white school was much closer. Her father joined an NAACP lawsuit. NAACP lawyer Thurgood Marshall argued the case (with four others combined) before the Supreme Court. All nine justices agreed: “separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” School segregation was unconstitutional.

clips.send: Freedom Rides. May 1961, Washington, D.C., the Deep South. The Supreme Court had banned segregation on interstate buses and in their stations, but Southern states ignored it. Black and white “Freedom Riders” rode buses together from Washington into the South to test the law. Near Anniston, Alabama, a mob burned one bus; riders were beaten in Birmingham and Montgomery. More riders kept coming. In September 1961 the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered segregation signs removed from bus stations.

clips.send: Memphis, 1968. 4 April 1968, Memphis, Tennessee. King went to Memphis to support Black sanitation workers on strike for fair pay and safe working conditions (“I AM A MAN” signs). On 4 April 1968 he was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel. He was 39. The nation mourned. A week later Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, banning discrimination in selling and renting homes. Today the motel is the National Civil Rights Museum.

clips.send: The Little Rock Nine. September 1957, Little Rock, Arkansas. Nine Black students enrolled at all-white Central High School to carry out the Brown decision. Arkansas Governor Orval Faubus sent the state National Guard to keep them out, and an angry crowd gathered. President Eisenhower sent soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division to escort the students — the federal government enforcing the Supreme Court’s ruling.

clips.send: The Birmingham Campaign. April–May 1963, Birmingham, Alabama. Birmingham was one of the most segregated cities in America. Protesters held marches and sit-ins, and boycotted downtown stores. Jailed for marching, King wrote the “Letter from Birmingham Jail”, explaining why people could not keep waiting for justice. In May, children and teenagers marched. Police used fire hoses and dogs on them. TV pictures shocked the nation; in June President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill. In September a bomb at the 16th Street Baptist Church killed four girls.

clips.send: Montgomery Bus Boycott. 5 Dec 1955 – 20 Dec 1956, Montgomery, Alabama. 1 December 1955: Rosa Parks refused to give her bus seat to a white man and was arrested. Black citizens stayed off the buses for 381 days. They walked, shared rides and organized a carpool system. A young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., led the Montgomery Improvement Association. In 1956 the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional; Montgomery’s buses were integrated in December 1956.

clips.send: Selma to Montgomery. March 1965, Selma, Montgomery, Alabama. In Selma, only a tiny share of Black adults were allowed to register to vote. On 7 March 1965 (“Bloody Sunday”), state troopers attacked peaceful marchers, led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams, on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Two weeks later, protected by federal troops, thousands marched 54 miles (87 km) to Montgomery. On 6 August 1965 Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act (《选举权法》).

clips.send: 格林斯伯勒静坐。1960年2月1日 · 北卡罗来纳州格林斯伯勒。四名黑人大学生坐在伍尔沃斯商店“只限白人”的午餐柜台前，礼貌地要求点餐。他们被拒绝了——第二天，他们带着更多同学回来了。几周之内，静坐抗议（sit-in）扩展到几十个城市。4月，学生们成立了学生非暴力协调委员会，S N C C。1960年7月，格林斯伯勒的伍尔沃斯柜台开始为黑人顾客服务。这段柜台的一部分如今收藏在史密森尼博物馆。

clips.send: 向华盛顿进军。1963年8月28日 · 华盛顿特区。约25万人聚集在林肯纪念堂前，参加“为工作和自由向华盛顿进军”——这是当时美国历史上规模最大的抗议之一。马丁·路德·金发表了“我有一个梦想”（I Have a Dream）演讲。年轻的约翰·刘易斯（后来成为佐治亚州的国会议员）也发表了讲话。这次进军为民权法案争取了支持。1964年7月2日，约翰逊总统签署《民权法案》（Civil Rights Act），禁止公共场所的种族隔离和就业歧视。

clips.send: 小石城九人。1957年9月 · 阿肯色州小石城。九名黑人学生到只收白人的中央中学入学，落实布朗案判决。阿肯色州州长福伯斯派州国民警卫队阻止他们进校，愤怒的人群聚集在学校外。艾森豪威尔总统派第101空降师的士兵护送学生上学——联邦政府用行动执行最高法院的判决。

clips.send: 自由乘车运动。1961年5月 · 从华盛顿特区到南方腹地。最高法院已经禁止州际公交车和车站实行隔离，但南方各州置之不理。黑人和白人“自由乘车者”一起乘公交车从华盛顿进入南方，检验法律是否被执行。在亚拉巴马州安尼斯顿附近，一辆公交车被暴徒烧毁；在伯明翰和蒙哥马利，乘车者遭到殴打。更多的人接着上车。1961年9月，州际商务委员会下令拆除车站里的隔离标牌。

clips.send: 从塞尔玛到蒙哥马利。1965年3月 · 亚拉巴马州塞尔玛至蒙哥马利。在塞尔玛，只有极少数黑人成年人被允许登记投票。1965年3月7日（“血腥星期日”），州警在埃德蒙·佩特斯桥上袭击了由约翰·刘易斯和霍齐亚·威廉斯带领的和平游行者。两周后，在联邦军队保护下，数千人步行54英里（87千米）到达蒙哥马利。1965年8月6日，约翰逊签署《选举权法》（Voting Rights Act）。

clips.send: 蒙哥马利公交车抵制运动。1955年12月5日—1956年12月20日 · 亚拉巴马州蒙哥马利。1955年12月1日，罗莎·帕克斯（Rosa Parks）拒绝把公交车座位让给一名白人男子，因而被捕。黑人市民381天不坐公交车：他们步行、搭车，还组织了拼车系统。年轻的牧师马丁·路德·金（Martin Luther King Jr.）领导了蒙哥马利进步协会。1956年，最高法院裁定公交车隔离违宪；12月，蒙哥马利的公交车取消了种族隔离。

clips.send: 伯明翰运动。1963年4—5月 · 亚拉巴马州伯明翰。伯明翰是美国种族隔离最严重的城市之一。抗议者举行游行、静坐，并抵制市中心的商店。金因游行被捕入狱，写下了《伯明翰狱中书简》，解释人们为什么不能再等待正义。5月，儿童和青少年走上街头。警察用高压水龙和警犬对付他们。电视画面震惊全国；6月，肯尼迪总统提出民权法案。9月，第十六街浸信会教堂发生爆炸，四名女孩遇难。

clips.send: 1968年的孟菲斯。1968年4月4日 · 田纳西州孟菲斯。金来到孟菲斯，支持为争取公平工资和安全工作条件而罢工的黑人环卫工人（他们举着“我是一个人”的标语）。1968年4月4日，金在洛林汽车旅馆遇刺身亡，年仅39岁。举国哀悼。一周后，国会通过《公平住房法》，禁止在买卖和租赁住房时进行歧视。今天，这家旅馆是国家民权博物馆。

clips.send: 布朗诉托皮卡教育委员会案。1954年5月17日 · 堪萨斯州托皮卡。黑人三年级女孩琳达·布朗离白人学校很近，却必须走很远去上黑人学校。她的父亲加入了全国有色人种协进会，N A A C P，发起的诉讼。NAACP的律师瑟古德·马歇尔（Thurgood Marshall）在最高法院为此案（与另外四个案子合并）辩护。九位大法官一致裁定：“隔离的教育设施本质上就是不平等的。”学校隔离违反宪法。
